result:
There is a strange freedom in being told "write about whatever you want."

Most writing has a purpose. An email needs to be answered. An essay needs to argue a point. A story needs to resolve. But when someone just says *write freely* - no prompt, no constraints, no destination - the blank page suddenly feels enormous. For a second you don't know where to start, because you could start anywhere.

So I will start here: with light.

I was thinking about light this morning, not in a physics sense, but in the way it behaves like a memory. The way 4pm light in October hits the side of a building and for a half-second you are ten years old again, walking home from school with your backpack half-unzipped. You weren't trying to remember anything. The light remembered for you.

We talk about light as if it reveals things, and it does. But it also erases. The brightest light washes everything out until it's just white. The dimmest light makes everything soft and uncertain at the edges. Maybe that's why we are so comforted by lamplight, by string lights, by candles - not the hard, honest light of noon that shows every flaw, but the forgiving light that says, you don't have to be fully seen to be here.

I think about an old lighthouse keeper I read about once. His job had been made obsolete by automation, but he still lived near the lighthouse. A journalist asked him if he missed the work. He said, "People think the light is for the ships. But most nights no ships came. I kept it on for the water itself. So it wouldn't be alone in the dark." I don't know if that story is true. I want it to be true.

We have built so many lighthouses that aren't made of stone.

The internet is one. A trillion little lights blinking on in bedrooms and offices and buses, each one saying *I am here. I am here. Do you see me?* We used to worry that the world would become too connected, that we would lose solitude. Now I think we worry about the opposite - that even while connected, we are still profoundly alone, shouting into a sea of other lights, hoping one beam finds us at the right angle.

And yet, sometimes it does.

Sometimes someone on the other side of the planet reads a sentence you wrote at 2 a.m. when you couldn't sleep and says, "I thought I was the only one who felt that." And for a moment two lights synchronize. That is no small thing. That is, in its own way, everything.

If I could write freely for 1000 words, I would want to waste some of them. I would want to not be efficient. So much of modern life is about efficiency - optimize your morning, optimize your inbox, optimize your workout. But free writing shouldn't be optimized. It should meander. It should take the long way home.

So let's take the long way.

Let's talk about kitchens at night. Not the curated kitchens from magazines, but lived-in kitchens. The one where the tile is chipped near the fridge and there's a drawer that always sticks. At midnight, after everyone else has gone to bed, a kitchen becomes a different country. The hum of the refrigerator is the national anthem. The clock ticks louder than it should. You stand there in socks, drinking water directly from a glass without a coaster, and you feel like the guardian of the house. Like your job is to keep watch while everyone else dreams. Do you know that feeling? That quiet, borrowed responsibility?

We don't talk enough about those small, sacred custodial moments. Holding the elevator for someone even though you're in a hurry. Watering a plant that isn't technically yours. Keeping the light on for the water.

Time does something strange in those moments. It stretches.

When I was a child, summers lasted forever. A single August afternoon contained an eternity - enough time to invent a game, get bored of it, invent another, have an argument, make up, and still be home before dinner. Now an entire year can pass in what feels like a blink. An entire month can disappear between paychecks and grocery runs.

I read that this is neurological. That children perceive time as slower because everything is new, so their brains write down more detailed memories. Adults live on autopilot, so the brain compresses the footage. Novelty stretches time; routine collapses it.

If that's true, then the secret to a longer life isn't to live more years, but to live more *first times*. To keep doing things you have never done before so your brain is forced to record in high definition again. Take a different route to work. Learn to make bread. Learn to say hello in a language you don't know. Talk to a stranger without checking your phone first. Get lost on purpose.

Because getting lost is underrated.

We have GPS now. We always know where we are, represented by a little blue dot. We never have to wonder, "Where am I?" But wondering where you are is an ancient, human question. Not just geographically, but existentially. Every folk tale is about someone who wanders into the woods and doesn't know the way back. The wandering *is* the story. If you know exactly where you're going, you're not on a journey, you're on a commute.

I like people who are willing to be commuters in their daily life but wanderers in their inner life. People who have a stable job and pay their rent but still read poetry that confuses them, still ask questions that have no answers, still look up at the sky and feel small in a good way.

Speaking of sky - have you ever really considered how strange it is that we live under a sky? That we are on a rock, spinning, held down by an invisible force, staring up at an endless blue that turns into endless black? We treat it as background. But if you stop and look for a full minute, really look, it becomes absurd and beautiful again. Clouds are just water taking a walk. The moon is always there even when we can't see it. The stars are old light finally arriving after traveling for millions of years just to land in your eye on a Tuesday. You are catching ancient light with your face.

That's worth a pause.

I think what I really want to say in these 1000 free words is this: Attention is a form of love.

What you pay attention to, you love. If you pay attention to resentment, you feed it. If you pay attention to beauty, even tiny beauty - the way someone's hands look when they are holding a mug, the sound of rain on an awning, the particular green of new leaves - you are practicing a kind of devotion.

We can't always control what happens to us. We can, to some degree, control what we notice. And what we notice, slowly, becomes our world.

So if you have read this far, wandering with me through light and lighthouses and midnight kitchens, thank you for lending me your attention for a little while. It is the most valuable thing you have, and you chose to spend it here, on these words that didn't have to be about anything, and so could be about everything.

Perhaps tomorrow you will be busy again. Perhaps there will be deadlines and dishes and notifications. But maybe, for a second, you will catch that 4 p.m. light on a building and you will let it remember something for you. Maybe you will stand in a kitchen at night and listen to the refrigerator hum and feel, for a moment, like the keeper of a small, important light.

Maybe you will keep it on, not because anyone is looking, but because the darkness shouldn't have to be alone.

And if no one has told you recently: your light is visible. Even when you doubt it. Even when you think it's too dim or too flickering or too ordinary. Somewhere, someone is navigating by it.

Keep it on.
